section_summary: Parker Pen Company complains that Japanese copies of its fountain pens are damaging sales across the Far East. Embassy and consular investigations initially fail to identify the makers, and officials question whether Parker has enforceable patent rights in Japan. Parker supplies further examples and presses for intervention; a later State Department memorandum considers approaching Japan’s Foreign Office.

people.name: William Phillips
people.role: State Department official signing for the Secretary of State

people.name: L. A. Crowell
people.role: inventor named on a patent assigned to Parker Pen Company

subfiles.title: Parker Pen Company letter on imitation pens
subfiles.from: Ivan D. Tefft, Parker Pen Company
subfiles.about: Tefft reports losses from Japanese imitation pens and encloses a SAFFRON pen instruction sheet.
subfiles.summary: Tefft says Parker cannot locate the infringers despite substantial expense and that its Far East business has suffered.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ambassador Grew concerning imitation Parker pens
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards Parker correspondence and requests action and a report.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Parker’s letters and the Department’s reply; asks Grew to investigate and report.

subfiles.title: Consulate General memorandum forwarding Kobe inquiry
subfiles.about: Garrels forwards Kobe’s response to the inquiry into alleged Parker patent and trademark violations.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a May 15 letter from the American Consulate at Kobe.

subfiles.title: Kobe Consulate report on Parker-style pens
subfiles.about: The Kobe Consulate reports that it cannot identify a Japanese maker of pens resembling Parker’s.
subfiles.summary: After canvassing its sources, the consulate asks Parker for a clue to the exporter.

subfiles.title: Embassy report on imitation Parker fountain pens
subfiles.about: Grew reports unsuccessful inquiries into Japanese production or export of imitation Parker pens.
subfiles.summary: Commercial and consular officers found neither the alleged pens nor their manufacturer. Grew concludes that Japanese authorities could not act without more specific information.

subfiles.title: George S. Parker’s appeal to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.about: Parker seeks help against Japanese pens allegedly copying the patented Vacumatic design.
subfiles.summary: Parker describes copied pens entering Far East markets and identifies Namiki advertising as a further concern. He says Japanese patent officials rejected protection for the transparent laminated barrel and encloses advertising and a Crowell patent.

subfiles.title: The Case of the Parker Pen Company
subfiles.about: An official assesses Parker’s patent claims and possible remedies.
subfiles.summary: The writer finds no basis for embassy intervention in Japan, distinguishes reputable Namiki from elusive small imitators, and suggests import restrictions where Parker holds patents or a trade agreement with Namiki.

subfiles.title: Note on replying to Parker’s letter
subfiles.about: The writer recommends a routine consular reply to Parker’s letter.
subfiles.summary: Recommends that the Consul General answer Parker’s inquiry using the supplied information.

subfiles.title: Consulate General reply to George S. Parker
subfiles.about: Garrels explains why the embassy and consulate see no local remedy for Parker’s complaint.
subfiles.summary: Garrels questions Parker’s ability to claim Japanese patent infringement, says Namiki holds patents for its filling device, and describes small producers as the source of many copies. He suggests action in countries where Parker has patents or a trade agreement with Namiki.

subfiles.title: Tefft’s response to Consul General Garrels
subfiles.from: Ivan D. Tefft, Parker Pen Company
subfiles.about: Tefft challenges the consular response and requests stronger State Department help against Japanese copies.
subfiles.summary: Tefft identifies Kawamoto’s General Fountain Pens and supplies catalogues and advertising for comparison. He disputes the explanation for rejection of Parker’s Japanese patent application, estimates lost Far East sales at $100,000 over eighteen months, and asks for effective intervention or procedural advice.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on further action
subfiles.about: The division considers whether the embassy should raise Parker’s case with Japan’s Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes the Commissioner of Patents’ doubt that Japanese decisions were discriminatory, making Parker’s case a weak example for intervention. It nevertheless suggests a diplomatic approach addressing broader American complaints about trademark infringements and asking whether rigid application of Japanese rules frustrates available remedies.
